No, sablefile 2.0 does not read `sablefile.lock` in the project root. Version 2.0 moves the lock file to a new place. The first 2.0 command that reads an older lock file handles it as described in lock-migration. [sec:install-upgrade]

Yes, there is a way to make `check` exit with status 0 even when a file has drifted in 2.0. Use the `--no-fail` flag with `sablefile check`. This flag ensures that the check exits with status 0 even when files have drifted, without changing which files are reported. [sec:no-fail-flag]
Yes, an ignore entry of `docs/**/*.tmp` will catch a file two folders down, like `docs/x/y/a.tmp`. [sec:ignore-recursive]

Yes, in 2.0, you can re-include something that an earlier ignore line had excluded by using a leading `!` to negate an earlier match, for example, `!keep.log` brings back a file that was previously excluded. [sec:ignore-syntax]
One line of the 1.0 lock file holds the SHA-256 hash of the file's content, two spaces, then the path. [sec:lockfile]

No, syncing the same content twice in 2.0 will not produce a different lock file each time. The lock file has no timestamps, and syncing the same content again produces an identical file. [sec:lockfile]
The count is fixed in 1.1, and no flag or setting changes it. [sec:remote-retries]
Pass `--retries 2` to sync. [sec:retries-flag]
The `[values]` table holds the values a placeholder can name. [sec:config-values]

`sablefile init` creates `sablefile.toml` in the folder where you run it, or in the folder you name. The new file has a `[values]` table with one entry, `project`, set to the folder name, and no `[[file]]` tables. [sec:init-command]

When a 2.0 command finds an older `sablefile.lock` and no `.sablefile/lock.json`, it reads the old file and prints a warning that names both files. If the command writes files, as `sync --apply` does, it also writes `.sablefile/lock.json` with each entry's SHA-256 hash, and keeps the mode where the old file has one. [sec:lock-migration]

No, init will not overwrite your config. It stops with an error if `sablefile.toml` already exists, so it never overwrites your configuration. [sec:init-command]
Yes, the 1.1 lock file cares about a file's mode. [sec:lock-mode]
In 2.0, entries use gitignore syntax. A line such as `*.log` matches at any depth. Therefore, `*.log` matches files in all folders, not just the top folder. [sec:ignore-syntax]
The docs don't say.

When a 2.0 command finds an older `sablefile.lock` and no `.sablefile/lock.json`, it reads the old file and prints a warning that names both files. If the command writes files, as `sync --apply` does, it also writes `.sablefile/lock.json` with each entry's SHA-256 hash and keeps the mode where the old file has one. A command that writes nothing leaves both files as they are. sablefile does not delete `sablefile.lock`; remove it yourself once the new file exists. [sec:lock-migration]

Yes, the 2.0 lock keeps each generated file's mode, the Unix permission bits such as `0644`, in `.sablefile/lock.json` [sec:lock-mode]. When a lock file is migrated from `sablefile.lock`, the mode is kept where the old file has one [sec:lock-migration].

Use the `--retries N` flag to set the number of times `sync` retries a failed fetch of a remote template, where N is a whole number less than or equal to 5. This flag controls the retry count for `sync` and applies only to that command. [sec:retries-flag]
No, sablefile check does not need a network connection to run. [sec:check-command]
No, `check` does not see changes on a remote template's server. [sec:remote-retries]

Run `sablefile check` after a sync. If no output appears, no generated file has drifted since the last sync. To see what drift looks like, open a generated file, change one line, and run the check again. The check prints `DRIFT` and the path of the file. Revert your edit to clear the message. The exit status for drift is described in check-exit-status. [sec:quickstart-check]

The mode that sablefile 1.1 stores for each generated file is the Unix permission bits, such as `0644` [sec:lock-mode]. The `sync` command stores this mode, as it records the mode of each file it writes [sec:lock-mode].

Run `sablefile diff` to preview sync's changes before writing. [sec:diff-command]

Yes, you can point `sablefile init` at a folder other than the current one. To do this, provide the path to the folder as an argument: `sablefile init path/to/folder`. The folder must already exist. [sec:init-directory]

No, sync --apply does not remove empty folders. sync never removes a folder, so empty folders you leave behind stay where they are. [sec:sync-create-dirs]
Template files can sit in any folder of the project. [sec:templates-location]
No, sablefile does not run any code that is inside a template. Rendering does not run code in the template. [sec:template-render]
Yes, a [[file]] table in 1.1 can take a template that lives at an https address. [sec:remote-templates]

If a remote template still cannot be fetched after the last retry, the command stops with an error that names the URL, and it exits with status 1. Targets that were not written keep their earlier lock entries. [sec:remote-fetch-failure]
Sync exits with status 1 when it cannot finish, for example when a template file is missing or a remote template cannot be fetched. [sec:sync-exit-status]

No, if sync exits with status 0, it only means that sync completed successfully, not that the generated text is what you want. You must open the generated files to verify their content. [sec:sync-exit-status]

You list paths for sablefile 1.0 to leave alone in the ignore file, `.sablefileignore`, which sits in the project root. Each entry is on a separate line, and blank lines are ignored. sync does not write an ignored target, check and diff skip it, and it gets no entry in the lock file. [sec:ignore-file]
No, with `--apply`, 2.0's sync does not write a target that is listed in the ignore file. [sec:ignore-file]
Lines that start with `#` are comments. [sec:ignore-syntax]
Look at the change before you act. Run `sablefile diff` to see how the file differs from its template. [sec:troubleshoot-drift]
Run `sablefile --version` to see the installed version. [sec:install-check-version]

To remove sablefile 1.0, run `python3 -m pip uninstall sablefile`. This removes the `sablefile` command and its package. It does not change your project. The configuration file, templates, generated files and lock file stay where they are. [sec:install-uninstall]

If the shell reports that `sablefile` is not found, the command is not installed in the environment that is active. Run `python3 -m pip show sablefile` in the same shell. If pip reports nothing, install the archive again. If pip reports a location but the command still does not run, the scripts folder of that environment is not on your path. Once the fault is fixed, run `sablefile --version`; see install-check-version. [sec:troubleshoot-command-not-found]
No, installing a new version of sablefile does not write any project file. [sec:install-upgrade]

A placeholder is a name in a template that sync replaces with a value, written as `{{project}}` in this version. A value is a string in the `[values]` table of the config file. [sec:glossary-terms]
No, the double-star pattern does not work in a sablefile 1.0 ignore file. The version 1.0 does not support `**`, and shell globs do not match across folders [sec:ignore-recursive].

No, the script will not fail because of the exit status. When check finds a drifted file, it prints `DRIFT` and the path and exits with status 0 [sec:check-exit-status]. Since the exit status is 0 even when files have drifted, a script cannot detect drift from the exit status in this version [sec:check-exit-status]. The script must read the printed lines to detect drift. [sec:check-exit-status]
Yes, the script will fail because the check command exits with status 1 when a file has drifted. [sec:check-exit-status]
No, the number of retries for a remote fetch cannot be set in sablefile 1.1. The retry count is fixed at 5 and cannot be changed via a flag or setting. [sec:remote-retries]

Yes, you can set the number of retries for a remote fetch in sablefile 2.0 using the `--retries N` flag, which applies to the `sync` and `diff` commands [sec:retries-flag]. This flag allows you to specify how many times a failed fetch of a remote template is retried, with a default of 5 retries [sec:remote-retries]. [sec:retries-flag]
The docs don't say.

No, in sablefile 2.0, `{{project}}` in a template does not get replaced by the project name. The double-brace form `{{project}}` is an error and fails to render; it must be changed to `${project}` before upgrading. [sec:placeholders]

No, after you change the template and run `sablefile sync --apply`, `sablefile check` will not report DRIFT for it. This is because `sync --apply` applies the changes to the generated file and updates the lock file to reflect the new content, so the generated file matches the template and the SHA-256 hash in the lock file. As a result, the next `sablefile check` will show no DRIFT [sec:drift-meaning].

No, `check` does not fetch anything and never retries, so it will not show changes if the server copy of your remote template changes [sec:remote-retries]. `diff` renders each `[[file]]` template and shows a unified diff between the rendered text and the file on disk, but it does not fetch the remote template from the server; thus, it will not reflect changes on the server copy [sec:diff-command]. Therefore, neither `check` nor `diff` will show changes if the server copy of the remote template changes.

No, a template does not have to sit inside the project folder. Template files can sit in any folder of the project, and the `template` key in a `[[file]]` table gives the path from the project folder [sec:templates-location].
Yes, you can stop check from failing when files have drifted by using the `--no-fail` flag. [sec:no-fail-flag]

No, sablefile does not need the network to run in 1.1. The `check` command works without a network connection because it reads the lock file and hashes each file without fetching remote templates or rendering templates [sec:check-command].

In a 1.0 [values] table, you should put strings, and each value must be enclosed in quotes because values are always strings [sec:config-values]. A number cannot go in as a bare value; it must be written in quotes [sec:config-values].

`--retries 0` disables retries for failed fetches during `sync`. This means that if a remote template fetch fails, `sync` will not attempt to retry and will give up immediately. This behavior is consistent with the description in [sec:retries-flag], which states that 0 means no retries. [sec:retries-flag]
